cka-exam-tips-2025.titleEn: CKA 2025: what I would have liked to know before taking the exam
cka-exam-tips-2025.excerptEn: I passed the CKA in March 2025 with a score of 91%. Here are my real prep notes: traps, speed tricks, and areas where people waste time.
cka-exam-tips-2025.contentEn:
Final score: **91%**. Remaining time: 8 minutes out of 120. Here's what I wish I knew.

## Exam Format (2025)

- **17 practical tasks** in a real terminal environment
- **120 minutes** (yes, it's short)
- **Minimum score**: 66%
- **Authorized documentation**: kubernetes.io/docs only
- **Domain weights**:

| Area | Weight |
|---|---|
| Storage | 10% |
| Troubleshooting | 30% |
| Workloads & Scheduling | 15% |
| Cluster Architecture | 25% |
| Services & Networking | 20% |

## Setting up your work environment

First thing to do at the start of the exam:

```bash
# Aliases
alias k=kubectl
export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
export now="--grace-period=0 --force"

# Auto-completion
source <(kubectl completion bash)
complete -F __start_kubectl k
```

These 4 lines will save you 15-20 minutes on the exam.

## Essential commands (never write YAML by hand)

```bash
# Pod
k run nginx --image=nginx $do > pod.yaml

# Deployment
k create deployment app --image=nginx --replicas=3 $do > deploy.yaml

# Service (expose a deployment)
k expose deployment app --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=ClusterIP $do > svc.yaml

# ConfigMap
k create configmap myconfig --from-literal=key=value $do

# Secret
k create secret generic mysecret --from-literal=password=s3cr3t $do

# ServiceAccount
k create serviceaccount mysa -n mynamespace $do

# Role + RoleBinding in one command
k create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods $do
k create rolebinding pod-reader-binding --role=pod-reader --user=alice $do
```

## Domain 1: Troubleshooting (30% -- most important)

This is where the exam is won or lost. Typical scenarios:

### Pod not starting

```bash
k describe pod <name>    # Check Events
k logs <pod>             # Container logs
k logs <pod> --previous  # Logs before last crash
```

### Node NotReady

```bash
k describe node <name>   # Conditions, events
ssh <node>               # If access is possible
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 50
```

### Network issue

```bash
# Check that endpoints exist
k get endpoints <service>

# Test DNS resolution
k run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup <service>.<namespace>

# Check NetworkPolicies
k get networkpolicies -A
```

## Domain 2: Cluster Architecture (25%)

What often comes up:

### ETCD backup & restore

```bash
# Backup
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/backup/etcd.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# Verify
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/backup/etcd.db

# Restore (remember the flags!)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/backup/etcd.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore
```

### Cluster Upgrade

```bash
# On the control plane
kubeadm upgrade plan
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.0

# Upgrade kubelet
apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubelet=1.29.0-1.1
systemctl restart kubelet

# On worker nodes
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# ... upgrade on node ...
kubectl uncordon <node>
```

## Domain 3: Storage (10%)

```bash
# PersistentVolume
k get pv,pvc -A

# Example PVC
k create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: my-pvc
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
  storageClassName: standard
EOF
```

## Classic traps

1. **Forgetting `-n <namespace>`**: 30% of tasks specify a non-default namespace.
2. **Not reading the full question**: there is often a kubectl context to switch with `kubectl config use-context`.
3. **Wasting time on a hard task**: if a task is worth 4% and takes 20 minutes, move on.
4. **Not checking your work**: after each task, do a `kubectl get` to confirm.

## Revision schedule (4 weeks)

| Week | Focus |
|---|---|
| W1 | Killer.sh mock exam 1 -- identify gaps |
| W2 | Review weak areas + practical labs |
| W3 | Killer.sh mock exam 2 + timing |
| W4 | Light revision, rest 2 days before the exam |

> **Killer.sh** (included in the certification) is harder than the real exam. If you can pass it, you're ready.

## Resources

- [Kubernetes Docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs) -- know how to navigate it by heart
- [Killer.sh](https://killer.sh) -- best exam simulator
- Personal taskfile with all my one-liners (published on this blog soon)

claude-code-devops-workflow-automatisati.titleEn: Claude Code in a DevOps workflow: what it really changes
claude-code-devops-workflow-automatisati.excerptEn: I have been using Claude Code for 3 months in my daily SRE. Here's what surprised me, what it replaces, and what it will never replace with concrete examples on GitLab pipelines, Kubernetes configs, and Terraform.
claude-code-devops-workflow-automatisati.contentEn:
I'm skeptical by default with "AI for dev" tools. Too many promises, too many demos on hello world. So when I started using Claude Code, I went into it without expectations just to see.

Three months later, it’s in my daily workflow. Here's why.

## What Claude Code really is

Claude Code is not a co-pilot who completes your lines. It's an agent that runs in your terminal, reads your codebase, executes commands, and works on complete tasks.

The practical difference:

- **Copilot**: you write `docker`, it completes `docker run -d --name...`
- **Claude Code**: you say "generate the Dockerfile for this Node.js app with multi-stage build and non-root user", he reads your `package.json`, writes the complete Dockerfile, and explains to you why he made each choice

```bash
# Installation
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# Lancer dans ton projet
claude
```

## The 3 modes which to use when

### Interactive mode (default)

Claude proposes each modification and awaits your approval. This is what I use for **everything related to production infrastructure**. I want to see every change before it is applied.

### Auto mode

Claude works independently, edits files directly. Useful for:
- Generate scaffolding (templates, boilerplate)
- Risk-free pure code refactoring
- Write tests

### Outline mode (`Shift+Tab` twice)

Claude thinks first, comes up with a plan, waits for your agreement, then executes. This is what I use for **complex multi-file tasks**. For example: "migrates this GitLab pipeline from the old syntax to the `needs:` rules + environment matrix".

## Real use cases which convinced me

### 1. Debugging GitLab pipelines

My most frequent case. A pipeline breaks, the error is cryptic, I paste the log into Claude Code:

```
"Ce job échoue avec : error: failed to solve: failed to read dockerfile:
open Dockerfile: no such file or directory. Le contexte Docker est ./services/api/"
```

In 10 seconds, Claude identifies that `context: ./services/api/` and `dockerfile: Dockerfile` is looking for the Dockerfile in `./services/api/Dockerfile`, while the Dockerfile is at the root. He proposes the fix and explains why not just the fix, the logic.

### 2. Generating Kubernetes manifests

I give a description:

> "Create a Deployment for a Python FastAPI app, 3 replicas, liveness probe on /health port 8000, requests 100m/128Mi limits 500m/512Mi, rolling update with maxUnavailable: 0"

Claude generates the complete, annotated YAML, ready to `kubectl apply`. What took 15 minutes of copying and pasting between docs and adjustments takes 30 seconds.

### 3. Writing Terraform modules

For repetitive patterns (creating a Terraform module for an S3 bucket with policy and versioning), Claude Code is unbeatable. It reads the existing context of your module, respects your naming conventions, and generates code consistent with what is already there.

### 4. Navigating an unknown codebase

When I take on a project that I haven't touched for 6 months:

```bash
"Explique le flux de l'authentification dans ce projet, depuis le middleware
jusqu'au stockage de session"
```

Claude reads the relevant files and gives you a structured summary. Not a generic doc an explanation based on **your** code.

## What it does not replace

Let's be honest.

**Architectural decisions**: Claude can offer you patterns, but deciding whether you shard MongoDB or not, whether you switch to microservices or not is your business context, your team, your budget. AI generates options, it does not decide.

**Deep understanding of incidents**: In P1, I don't want a probabilistic suggestion. I want facts. Claude Code can help me go faster (generates a PromQL query, explains a stack trace), but the causal analysis remains human.

**Implicit knowledge**: Claude does not know that your Kubernetes cluster has a quirk with PodDisruptionBudgets because of a specific operator version. This knowledge is in the heads of the team and the post-mortems.

## Configuration CLAUDE.md the investment that changes everything

The `CLAUDE.md` file at the root of the project is read by Claude at startup. This is where you give it the permanent context:

```markdown
# CLAUDE.md

## Stack
- Kubernetes 1.29 sur Fly.io
- GitLab CI/CD avec runners partagés
- Terraform 1.7 + Terraform Cloud

## Conventions
- Toutes les ressources Terraform dans modules/
- Variables dans variables.tf, outputs dans outputs.tf
- Nommage: {env}-{service}-{ressource}

## À ne jamais faire
- Ne jamais modifier les fichiers .tfstate directement
- Ne jamais hardcoder de secrets (utiliser Vault)
- Ne pas utiliser `kubectl apply` sans `--dry-run=client` d'abord
```

With this, Claude respects your conventions without you having to remind them each session.

## Verdict after 3 months

Claude Code made me faster on repetitive tasks and code generation. It saved me probably 1-2 hours per day on plumbing tasks (writing configs, syntax debugging, code navigation).

What it didn't make me better at my job. That's the field experience, the post-mortems, and the hours spent debugging problems that no one had documented.

The tool amplifies what you already know how to do. It does not replace skill.

---

*Claude Code is available via `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. The VS Code extension is in beta and works well for those who prefer a graphical interface.*

debugging-oom-kill-kubernetes.titleEn: Hunting an OOMKill at 2 a.m.: methodology and kubectl one-liners
debugging-oom-kill-kubernetes.excerptEn: A pod that restarts every 5 minutes. Empty logs. A screaming pager. Here's how I tracked down and fixed an OOMKill in production without losing my mind.
debugging-oom-kill-kubernetes.contentEn:
It's 2:17 a.m. My phone vibrates. PagerDuty alert: `CrashLoopBackOff` on the payment service. The kind of alert that wakes everyone up except the monster who caused it.

Here is how I solved this problem step by step.

## Step 1: Initial screening

The first command to run when a pod crashes:

```bash
kubectl get pods -n payments -l app=payment-svc --watch
```

We see the restarts piling up. Then:

```bash
kubectl describe pod -n payments -l app=payment-svc | grep -A5 "Last State"
```

The output reveals:

```
Last State:  Terminated
  Reason:    OOMKilled
  Exit Code: 137
  Started:   Wed, 15 Jan 2025 02:12:03 +0000
  Finished:  Wed, 15 Jan 2025 02:17:41 +0000
```

Exit code **137** = OOMKill. The container has exceeded its memory limit.

## Step 2: Understand memory consumption

```bash
# Consommation actuelle
kubectl top pods -n payments --sort-by=memory

# Voir les limits/requests configurées
kubectl get pod -n payments -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].resources}{"\n"}{end}'
```

Shocking result: `limits.memory: 256Mi` for a Java service. Someone had copied and pasted the config of a Go microservice without adjusting.

## Step 3: Analyze historical metrics

With Prometheus/Grafana, we look for the pattern:

```promql
container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="payments", container="payment-svc"}
/ container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{namespace="payments", container="payment-svc"}
```

The ratio has been close to 0.98 for 3 days. The JVM inflated its heap with each nighttime traffic peak.

## Step 4: Recover the logs before the crash

The logs of the crashed pod are no longer there but those of the previous container are:

```bash
kubectl logs -n payments -l app=payment-svc --previous --tail=200
```

We find the fatal lines:

```
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded
  at java.util.Arrays.copyOf(Arrays.java:3210)
  ...
```

## Step 5: Fix and validation

Memory limit patch:

```bash
kubectl patch deployment payment-svc -n payments --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"1Gi"},
       {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/memory","value":"512Mi"}]'
```

And added JVM flags to constrain the heap:

```yaml
env:
  - name: JAVA_OPTS
    value: "-Xms512m -Xmx768m -XX:+UseContainerSupport"
```

## Lessons learned

| Antipattern | Good practice |
|---|---|
| Copy and paste resource limits | Profile each service separately |
| Limits = Requests | Requests = p50 usage, Limits = p99 + margin |
| Ignore memory metrics | Alert at 80% of the limit |

> **Golden rule**: for the JVM in K8s, always use `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` (JDK 10+). Without this, the JVM sees the node's RAM, not the container's.

## Useful one-liners to keep

```bash
# Tous les pods OOMKilled du cluster
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.status.containerStatuses[]?.lastState.terminated.reason=="OOMKilled") | .metadata.name'

# Memory pressure par nœud
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A3 "Conditions:"

# Top consumers
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head -20
```

2:47. The service is stable. I'm going back to bed.

github-actions-kubernetes-cicd.titleEn: CI/CD to Kubernetes with GitHub Actions: the pipeline I wish I had from the start
github-actions-kubernetes-cicd.excerptEn: How to build a robust Kubernetes deployment pipeline with GitHub Actions: build, scan, progressive deployment, and automatic rollback. Zero compromise on security.
github-actions-kubernetes-cicd.contentEn:
After seeing a dozen "functional but fragile" pipelines in business, I decided to write the version I would have wanted to have from the start.

## Pipeline architecture

```
PR ouverte → lint + tests unitaires
PR mergée (main) → build image → scan sécurité → push → déploiement staging
Tag v* → déploiement production avec canary
```

## Repo structure

```
.github/
  workflows/
    ci.yml           # Tests + lint
    cd-staging.yml   # Deploy automatique sur staging
    cd-production.yml # Deploy production sur tag
  actions/
    deploy/          # Action composite réutilisable
k8s/
  base/              # Kustomize base
  overlays/
    staging/
    production/
```

## CI workflow (testing)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'
      
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test -- --coverage
      
      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4

  build-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Verify Docker build
        run: docker build --target builder -t test-build .
```

## CD to staging workflow

```yaml
# .github/workflows/cd-staging.yml
name: Deploy to Staging

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
      security-events: write
    
    outputs:
      image-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
      image-tag: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      
      - name: Extract metadata
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        with:
          images: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}
          tags: |
            type=sha,prefix=sha-
            type=ref,event=branch
      
      - name: Build and push
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
      
      # Scan de sécurité sur l'image buildée
      - name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          format: 'sarif'
          output: 'trivy-results.sarif'
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
          exit-code: '1'  # Fail le pipeline si CRITICAL trouvé
      
      - name: Upload Trivy scan results
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with:
          sarif_file: 'trivy-results.sarif'

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Setup kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
      
      - name: Configure kubeconfig
        run: |
          mkdir -p ~/.kube
          echo "${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_STAGING }}" | base64 -d > ~/.kube/config
          chmod 600 ~/.kube/config
      
      - name: Deploy with Kustomize
        run: |
          cd k8s/overlays/staging
          kustomize edit set image app=${{ needs.build-and-push.outputs.image-tag }}
          kubectl apply -k .
      
      - name: Wait for rollout
        run: |
          kubectl rollout status deployment/app -n staging --timeout=5m
      
      - name: Smoke test
        run: |
          sleep 10
          STATUS=$(curl -sf https://staging.example.com/health | jq -r '.status')
          [ "$STATUS" = "ok" ] || exit 1
```

## Automatic rollback

```yaml
      - name: Rollback on failure
        if: failure()
        run: |
          kubectl rollout undo deployment/app -n staging
          echo "::error::Deploy failed   rolled back to previous version"
```

## Secure secrets

```bash
# Encoder le kubeconfig pour GitHub Secrets
cat ~/.kube/config | base64 | pbcopy
# → coller dans Settings > Secrets > KUBECONFIG_STAGING
```

And in the kubeconfig config, use a **dedicated ServiceAccount** with minimal RBAC:

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: staging
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "patch", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "services"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
```

## What I would have added from the start

1. **Scan for secrets** in the code (`gitleaks` or `trufflesecurity`)
2. Automatic **SBOM** with each release
3. **Slack notifications** on prod deployment failure
4. **Smoke more robust tests** not just a `/health`

> The best pipeline is the one your team can debug at 3 a.m. Keep it readable.

gitlab-cicd-full-iac-devsecops.titleEn: GitLab CI/CD Full IaC: Terraform + Ansible + DevSecOps integrated complete architecture
gitlab-cicd-full-iac-devsecops.excerptEn: How we built a GitLab pipeline that deploys Terraform infrastructure, configures servers with Ansible, scans images with Trivy, and generates an SBOM/SLSA without sacrificing dev speed.
gitlab-cicd-full-iac-devsecops.contentEn:
The subject constantly comes up in DevOps discussions: “we want to do IaC, but the pipelines are too slow” or “we added security scans and now no one is pushing anything anymore”. Here's how we solved both in production.

## Overall pipeline architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    GitLab Pipeline                           │
├──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬─────────────────┤
│  lint &  │ terraform│ security │  ansible │    deploy       │
│  validate│  plan    │  scan    │  staging │    prod         │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴─────────────────┘
     │           │          │          │            │
  <30s        <2min      <3min      <5min      manuel (prod)
```

Absolute rule: **the pipeline must finish in < 12 minutes** on a regular MR, otherwise the devs bypass. We measured, established pipeline SLOs, and alerted on them as on any service.

## Stage 1: Lint & Validate (< 30 seconds)

The first internship must be dazzling. If we fail here, the dev fixes it in 30 seconds and pushes back.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - validate
  - plan
  - security
  - deploy-staging
  - deploy-prod

variables:
  TF_VERSION: "1.7.0"
  ANSIBLE_VERSION: "9.0.0"
  TF_ROOT: ${CI_PROJECT_DIR}/terraform
  ANSIBLE_ROOT: ${CI_PROJECT_DIR}/ansible

.terraform_base:
  image: hashicorp/terraform:${TF_VERSION}
  before_script:
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} init -backend=false

tf:validate:
  extends: .terraform_base
  stage: validate
  script:
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} validate
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} fmt -check -recursive
  rules:
    - changes:
        - terraform/**/*

ansible:lint:
  image: cytopia/ansible-lint:latest
  stage: validate
  script:
    - ansible-lint ${ANSIBLE_ROOT}/playbooks/
  rules:
    - changes:
        - ansible/**/*
```

The `rules: changes:` is fundamental, we only validate what has changed. On a monorepo with 20 teams, without this filter the pipeline runs for everyone on each commit.

## Stage 2: Terraform Plan with automatic MR comment

The Terraform plan is posted as a comment on the MR. Reviewers see exactly what will change without having to clone and launch the plan themselves.

```yaml
tf:plan:
  extends: .terraform_base
  stage: plan
  environment:
    name: staging
  script:
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} init
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} plan 
        -var-file="environments/${CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME}.tfvars"
        -out=${TF_ROOT}/tfplan
        -no-color 2>&1 | tee /tmp/plan.txt
    - |
      # Post le plan en commentaire MR
      if [ -n "$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID" ]; then
        COMMENT="## Terraform Plan   ${CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME}\n\`\`\`\n$(cat /tmp/plan.txt | tail -30)\n\`\`\`"
        curl -s --request POST \
          --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: ${GITLAB_API_TOKEN}" \
          --data-urlencode "body=${COMMENT}" \
          "${CI_API_V4_URL}/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/merge_requests/${CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID}/notes"
      fi
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - ${TF_ROOT}/tfplan
    expire_in: 1 hour
```

## Stage 3: DevSecOps Trivy, Vault, SBOM

This is where a lot of pipelines become slow. Our optimizations:

### Trivy with cache

```yaml
security:trivy:
  image: aquasec/trivy:latest
  stage: security
  variables:
    TRIVY_CACHE_DIR: ${CI_PROJECT_DIR}/.trivycache
  cache:
    key: trivy-db
    paths:
      - ${CI_PROJECT_DIR}/.trivycache
  script:
    # Scan de l'image Docker buildée
    - trivy image
        --exit-code 1
        --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
        --ignore-unfixed
        --format json
        --output trivy-report.json
        ${CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE}:${CI_COMMIT_SHA}
    # Scan IaC Terraform
    - trivy config
        --exit-code 0
        --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
        ${TF_ROOT}/
  artifacts:
    reports:
      container_scanning: trivy-report.json
    paths:
      - trivy-report.json
    when: always
```

**`--ignore-unfixed`** is non-negotiable in practice. CVEs without available fixes create noise and unjustified blockages. We alert on unfixed separately, asynchronously, not by blocking the pipeline.

### Secrets with HashiCorp Vault

```yaml
.vault_secrets:
  id_tokens:
    VAULT_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://vault.cegedim.internal
  secrets:
    DATABASE_PASSWORD:
      vault: secret/data/prod/mongodb@cegedim
      file: false
    ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD:
      vault: secret/data/ci/ansible@cegedim
      file: false
```

Authentication is done via JWT (GitLab OIDC → Vault), zero static secrets in CI variables. GitLab's JWT token has a lifespan of 300 seconds, enough for the job, not enough to be exfiltrated.

### SBOM Generation

```yaml
security:sbom:
  image: anchore/syft:latest
  stage: security
  script:
    - syft ${CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE}:${CI_COMMIT_SHA}
        --output cyclonedx-json=sbom.json
        --output spdx-json=sbom-spdx.json
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - sbom.json
      - sbom-spdx.json
    expire_in: 90 days
```

The SBOM is archived for 90 days, enough to respond to audits and trace the components in the event of a CVE discovered subsequently (Log4Shell case).

## Stage 4: Ansible on Staging

```yaml
ansible:staging:
  image: cytopia/ansible:${ANSIBLE_VERSION}
  stage: deploy-staging
  environment:
    name: staging
  before_script:
    - echo "${ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD}" > /tmp/.vault_pass
    - eval $(ssh-agent -s)
    - echo "${SSH_PRIVATE_KEY}" | tr -d '\r' | ssh-add -
  script:
    - ansible-playbook
        --inventory ${ANSIBLE_ROOT}/inventories/staging/
        --vault-password-file /tmp/.vault_pass
        --diff
        --check  # dry-run d'abord
        ${ANSIBLE_ROOT}/playbooks/site.yml
    - ansible-playbook
        --inventory ${ANSIBLE_ROOT}/inventories/staging/
        --vault-password-file /tmp/.vault_pass
        --diff
        ${ANSIBLE_ROOT}/playbooks/site.yml
  after_script:
    - rm -f /tmp/.vault_pass
```

The double pass (`--check` then real) avoids unpleasant surprises. If the check fails, the job fails without deploying anything.

## Deploy Prod: protection by GitLab environment

```yaml
terraform:apply:prod:
  extends: .terraform_base
  stage: deploy-prod
  environment:
    name: production
  when: manual
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
  script:
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} init
    - terraform -chdir=${TF_ROOT} apply
        -var-file="environments/production.tfvars"
        -auto-approve
        ${TF_ROOT}/tfplan
```

The `when: manual` + protection of the GitLab environment (reviewers required) = double human validation before any infra change in prod. Approval is done in GitLab, with complete audit trail.

## What really accelerated the pipeline

| Optimization | Profit |
|---|---|
| Cache Trivy DB | -90s per job |
| `rules: changes:` per folder | -40% of useless jobs |
| Parallel matrix for multi-env | -3min on plans |
| Dedicated runner (no shared) | -1min scheduling |
| Pre-built Docker image with tools | -45s setup |

The total went from 28 minutes to 11 minutes on the full pipeline. The devs stopped complaining.

---

The complete template for this pipeline is available in the GitLab CI/CD Full IaC course.

kubectl-cheatsheet-prod.excerptEn: The kubectl commands that I really use in production, classified by emergency situation. No theory, just what works.
kubectl-cheatsheet-prod.contentEn:
This is not yet another kubectl tutorial. These are the commands that I have in my snippets because they saved my production.

## Quick diagnosis

```bash
# Vue d'ensemble immédiate
kubectl get pods,svc,deploy,ingress -n <ns> -o wide

# Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30

# Pod qui refuse de démarrer
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> | tail -40

# Logs en temps réel multi-pods
kubectl logs -n <ns> -l app=<name> -f --max-log-requests=10
```

## Access and debug

```bash
# Shell dans un pod
kubectl exec -it <pod> -n <ns> -- /bin/sh

# Sans shell dans l'image ? Ephemeral container (K8s 1.23+)
kubectl debug -it <pod> -n <ns> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>

# Copier un fichier depuis/vers un pod
kubectl cp <ns>/<pod>:/app/logs/error.log ./error.log
kubectl cp ./config.yaml <ns>/<pod>:/tmp/config.yaml

# Port-forward pour tester en local
kubectl port-forward -n <ns> svc/<service> 8080:80
```

## Quick manipulations

```bash
# Restart d'un deployment sans downtime
kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> -n <ns>

# Scale rapide
kubectl scale deployment/<name> -n <ns> --replicas=0
kubectl scale deployment/<name> -n <ns> --replicas=3

# Rollback au déploiement précédent
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> -n <ns>

# Voir l'historique
kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> -n <ns>
```

## Labels and selectors

```bash
# Ajouter un label
kubectl label pod <pod> -n <ns> debug=true

# Retirer un label
kubectl label pod <pod> -n <ns> debug-

# Trouver tous les pods avec un label
kubectl get pods -A -l env=production,tier=frontend
```

## Resources and quotas

```bash
# Consommation CPU/RAM
kubectl top pods -n <ns> --sort-by=cpu
kubectl top nodes

# Vérifier les quotas d'un namespace
kubectl describe resourcequota -n <ns>
kubectl describe limitrange -n <ns>

# Quels pods mangent le plus de CPU sur le cluster ?
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu | head -15
```

## Secrets and ConfigMaps

```bash
# Voir un secret décodé
kubectl get secret <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.data}' | \
  jq 'to_entries[] | .key + ": " + (.value | @base64d)'

# Créer un secret depuis un fichier
kubectl create secret generic <name> \
  --from-file=tls.crt=./cert.pem \
  --from-file=tls.key=./key.pem \
  -n <ns>

# Hot-reload d'un configmap (avec annotation)
kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> -n <ns>
```

## Network debug

```bash
# Tester la connectivité depuis un pod temporaire
kubectl run netcheck --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -v http://my-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local:8080/health

# Vérifier les endpoints d'un service
kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns>

# DNS resolution
kubectl run dnscheck --rm -it --image=busybox -- \
  nslookup my-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local
```

## Cleaning

```bash
# Supprimer tous les pods Failed/Completed
kubectl delete pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed
kubectl delete pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Succeeded

# Forcer la suppression d'un pod bloqué en Terminating
kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns> --grace-period=0 --force

# Nettoyer les images sur tous les nœuds (à faire avec prudence)
kubectl get nodes -o name | xargs -I{} kubectl debug {} --image=alpine \
  -- sh -c "crictl rmi --prune"
```

## Aliases to put in your .bashrc

```bash
alias k='kubectl'
alias kgp='kubectl get pods'
alias kgpa='kubectl get pods -A'
alias kdp='kubectl describe pod'
alias klf='kubectl logs -f'
alias kex='kubectl exec -it'
alias kns='kubectl config set-context --current --namespace'
```

## My multi-cluster kubeconfig config

```bash
# Lister les contextes
kubectl config get-contexts

# Changer de contexte
kubectl config use-context production-eu-west-1

# Contexte courant
kubectl config current-context

# Fusionner deux kubeconfigs
KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config-prod:~/.kube/config-staging \
  kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/config
```

> **Tip**: I use [kubectx + kubens](https://github.com/ahmetb/kubectx) to switch context/namespace in one command. Essential when managing 10+ clusters.

mongodb-ops-manager-ha-production.titleEn: MongoDB Ops Manager HA in production: replica sets, sharding and PBM what we don't tell you
mongodb-ops-manager-ha-production.excerptEn: 18 months operating MongoDB 8.0 with Ops Manager on a mission-critical PaaS platform. Here are the real architectural decisions, the pitfalls of sharding, and why PBM replaced mongodump in our backup strategy.
mongodb-ops-manager-ha-production.contentEn:
When I was given responsibility for the MongoDB platform in production, the cluster was running standalone with `mongodump` backups planned via cron. Functional. Fragile. Not scalable.

18 months later: multi-AZ replica sets, sharding on critical collections, Ops Manager 8.0 with complete automation, and PBM for consistent millisecond backups. Here's what I learned.

## Why Ops Manager rather than Cloud Manager

The question comes up often. For an on-premises hosted PaaS platform with data sovereignty constraints, Cloud Manager (SaaS Mongo Atlas) was not an option. Ops Manager is installed internally, manages deployment automation, rolling updates, backups, and alerts from a centralized interface.

What the doc doesn't say: **Ops Manager itself must be highly available**. We started with a standalone Ops Manager, and this was the first point of failure that we corrected. The final architecture:

```
Ops Manager (3 nœuds actif/passif/arbitre)
    └── Application Database : MongoDB 3-node replica set dédié
    └── Backup Daemon : 2 instances avec stockage S3-compatible
```

## Replica Sets: the parameters that change everything in production

The default deployment of a replica set works. In production, there are three parameters that we systematically adjust.

**`oplogSizeMB`** By default, the oplog is 5% of disk space or 1GB. On write-intensive workloads (our case with OpenSearch), an oplog that is too small causes secondary lag and then complete resynchronization. We set it to 50GB.

**`votes` and `priority`** In a multi-AZ deployment with two datacenters, we add an arbiter in a third site. The referee does not store data but participates in the election. Warning: an arbiter with `votes: 1` can block an election if the two main DCs lose connectivity between them. We use `priority: 0` on the secondary of the secondary DC to force promotion to the correct DC.

**`readPreference`** On analytics requests and exports, we route to `secondaryPreferred`. This relieves the primary and the analytics latencies go from 2-3s to 400-500ms.

```javascript
// Connection string pour l'analytique
mongodb://user:pass@primary:27017,sec1:27017,sec2:27017/db
  ?replicaSet=rs0
  &readPreference=secondaryPreferred
  &readPreferenceTags=dc:secondary
```

## Sharding: when and how

We didn't shard right away. **Premature sharding is the classic error** it adds operational complexity (mongos, config servers) without benefit on collections < 50GB.

We sharded when two conditions were met:
1. A collection exceeded 100GB with slow queries despite indexes
2. The access patterns were clear (no scatter-gather on the shard key)

The choice of the shard key is critical and irreversible (before MongoDB 5.0 at least). We opted for a **compound shard key** `{ tenantId: 1, createdAt: 1 }` rather than a hashized `_id`. Why:
- Queries almost always filter by `tenantId`
- Avoids scatter-gather in 90% of cases
- The distribution is balanced because the tenants have comparable volumes

```javascript
sh.shardCollection("proddb.events", { tenantId: 1, createdAt: 1 })
```

Classic trap: **jumbo chunks**. If a tenant generates 20% of the volume, its chunks can no longer be migrated. Solution: pre-split before loading, and `refineCollectionShardKey` in MongoDB 4.4+ to add a dimension.

## PBM (Percona Backup for MongoDB) vs mongodump

`mongodump` has two fundamental problems in production:

1. **Not consistent on a sharded cluster** each shard is dumped independently, cross-shard transactions are not atomic in the backup
2. **Not incremental** each backup is a full one, therefore slow and storage intensive

PBM solves both. It uses oplog to create **consistent point-in-time backups** across the entire cluster. Our setup:

```yaml
# pbm-config.yaml
storage:
  type: s3
  s3:
    region: fr-east-1
    bucket: mongo-backups-prod
    credentials:
      access-key-id: ${AWS_ACCESS_KEY}
      secret-access-key: ${AWS_SECRET_KEY}

backup:
  compression: pgzip
  compressionLevel: 6
```

**Planning:**
- Full backup: Sunday 02:00
- Oplog continuous shipping (PITR activated) restoration possible at any point in the last 7 days
- Retention: 4 fulls + oplog

To test the restoration (what everyone forgets to do):

```bash
# Restauration sur environnement de test, pas prod
pbm restore --time "2026-04-14T10:30:00" \
  --base-snapshot "2026-04-13T02:00:00.123456789Z"
```

We do a monthly automatic restoration test via a GitLab CI job which restores to the staging environment and checks the integrity of the data.

## Alerting: the metrics that really matter

Prometheus + Grafana collect metrics via `mongodb_exporter`. The alerts we have in production:

| Metric | Threshold | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `mongodb_rs_members_health` | < 1 | Member down |
| `mongodb_rs_replication_lag_seconds` | > 30s | Secondary late |
| `mongodb_connections_current` | > 80% of max | Saturation connections |
| `mongodb_op_latencies_latency` (write) | p99 > 100ms | Performance issue |
| PBM backup status | != "done" after window | Backup failed |

The replication lag trap: an alert that goes off at 3 a.m. because of an index build in the background. Added an exception for current `createIndexes`.

## What we would do differently

**Ops Manager in Kubernetes**: we installed it on VMs. In hindsight, the MongoDB Enterprise Operator Kubernetes would have simplified lifecycle management. But the migration from Ops Manager to the K8s operator is non-trivial and is an ongoing project.

**Oplog monitoring** from the start: we had a resynchronization incident at 2 a.m. because the oplog window had fallen to 4 hours following a write spike. Now we alert at < 12 p.m. oplog window.

**Automated recovery tests**: we added it after the first real incident, not before. The backup test is worthless if you don't test the restoration.

---

If you are implementing MongoDB in production and have questions about architecture or sizing, comments are open.

observabilite-prometheus-grafana-loki-gu.titleEn: Monitoring ≠ Observability: building the Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo stack
observabilite-prometheus-grafana-loki-gu.excerptEn: Everyone says 'we have Grafana, so we are watchable'. Fake. Here is the real difference between monitoring and observability, and how to build a real stack of the three pillars of metrics, logs, traces with open source tools.
observabilite-prometheus-grafana-loki-gu.contentEn:
The phrase I hear most often during infrastructure audits: “we have Grafana, so we have observability”. This is false, and the difference is not semantic, it changes what we are capable of doing during an incident.

## Monitoring vs Observability the real difference

**monitoring** answers pre-defined questions:
- CPU > 80%?
- Error rate > 1%?
- Pod in CrashLoopBackOff?

You anticipated these questions **before** the incident. You created the alerts. If something new breaks, something you didn't anticipate, monitoring doesn't tell you anything.

**Observability** answers ad-hoc questions that you ask during the incident:
- Why this timeout request for this specific user?
- What changed between 2:00 p.m. and 2:05 p.m.?
- Which service calls which other service with how much latency?

The analogy I use in training: monitoring is the fire alarm. She tells you there is a fire. Observability is the camera that shows you where the fire is, how it started, and what path it follows.

## The three pillars

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     OBSERVABILITÉ                           │
├──────────────┬─────────────────┬───────────────────────────┤
│   MÉTRIQUES  │      LOGS       │         TRACES            │
│  Prometheus  │      Loki       │    Tempo / Jaeger         │
│              │                 │                           │
│  CPU, RAM    │  "ERROR 500 at  │  req → service A → B → C │
│  latence p99 │   14:03 user X" │  latence par span         │
│  taux d'err  │  stack traces   │  bottleneck exact         │
└──────────────┴─────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘
                        │
                        ▼
                    GRAFANA
           (visualisation unifiée de tout)
                        │
                        ▼
                ALERTMANAGER
         (email, Slack, PagerDuty, Teams)
```

### Why all three? Not just one?

Each pillar answers a different type of question. A real incident requires all three:

> **Alert**: p99 latency > 2s on `/api/orders` (Prometheus → Alertmanager)
>
> **Observation**: it has been going on since 2:03 p.m., correlated with a deployment (Grafana Metrics)
>
> **Cause**: the logs show `SQLException: connection pool exhausted` on the `order-service` service (Loki)
>
> **Root cause**: the trace shows that `order-service` calls `inventory-service` 47 times per request instead of 1 regression in the cache (Tempo)

Without the traces, you would have searched on the DB side for 45 minutes.

## Deployment architecture (Kubernetes)

```yaml
# architecture simplifiée
namespace: monitoring
  - prometheus (scrape toutes les métriques)
  - alertmanager (routing des alertes)
  - grafana (visualisation)
  - loki (aggregation des logs)
  - promtail (agent de collecte logs, sur chaque node)
  - tempo (backend de tracing)
  - otel-collector (OpenTelemetry Collector   normalisation des traces)
```

### Prometheus

Prometheus scrapes `/metrics` endpoints exposed by your services. It works in pull mode; it is he who fetches the metrics, not your services which push them.

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'kubernetes-pods'
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
    relabel_configs:
      # Ne scraper que les pods annotés
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
        action: keep
        regex: true
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port]
        action: replace
        target_label: __address__
        regex: (.+)
        replacement: ${1}:${2}
```

Absolute rule: **annotate your pods** for scraping, no static configuration. When you have 200+ services, a static list is unmaintainable.

```yaml
# Dans ton Deployment
metadata:
  annotations:
    prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
    prometheus.io/port: "8080"
    prometheus.io/path: "/metrics"
```

### Loki Logs without index

The architectural difference of Loki vs Elasticsearch: **no index on log content**. Loki only indexes labels (namespace, pod, container, etc.). The content is compressed and stored raw.

Practical consequence: Loki is 10x cheaper to operate than Elasticsearch for log storage. But full-text queries are slower if you haven't filtered by labels first.

```logql
# LogQL   requête Loki
# Toujours filtrer par label D'ABORD, puis par contenu
{namespace="production", app="api-gateway"} 
  |= "ERROR" 
  | json 
  | line_format "{{.level}} {{.msg}}"
  | rate[5m]
```

**Classic trap:** make a query on `{namespace="production"}` without additional filter on large volumes. You will scan GB of compressed logs. Always add the most selective label first.

### Distributed Tempo Tracing

Tempo is the trace backend from Grafana Labs. It is OpenTelemetry, Zipkin, and Jaeger compatible so you don't have to choose a tracing format.

```yaml
# otel-collector-config.yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

exporters:
  otlp/tempo:
    endpoint: tempo:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp/tempo]
```

In your application (Python example):

```python
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

provider = TracerProvider()
exporter = OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint="http://otel-collector:4317")
provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(exporter))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def get_order(order_id: str):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("get_order") as span:
        span.set_attribute("order.id", order_id)
        # ... ta logique
```

## Correlation where it becomes real observability

Prometheus, Loki and Tempo separately, it's still improved monitoring. What creates real observability is the **correlation** between the three in Grafana.

**Exemplified Logs**: in a Tempo trace, clicking on a span directly opens the corresponding Loki logs for this service, at this precise timestamp.

**Service Graph**: automatically generated from the traces, it shows the dependencies between services and their P50/P95/P99 latencies.

**Correlated alerts**: a Prometheus alert can point to a Grafana dashboard which simultaneously displays the metrics AND logs of the service in question.

```
[ALERTE] latence > 2s sur order-service
  └── Lien : Grafana dashboard → timeline incident
        ├── Métriques : spike de connexions DB à 14h03
        ├── Logs : "connection pool exhausted" → 47 occurrences
        └── Traces : span DB bloque 1.8s sur inventory-service
```

This sequence, without searching, without manually crossing, that's operational observability.

## What we implemented in production

Our current stack runs on Kubernetes with:
- Prometheus Operator (CRDs for declarative configuration)
- Loki in distributed mode (high availability, S3 object storage)
- Tempo with S3 backend
- Grafana with data sources configured via Terraform (no click-click)
- Prometheus alerts → Alertmanager → Zoom Chat (via custom webhook)

The last part alerts in Zoom Chat increased our MTTD (Mean Time To Detect) from 12 minutes to 3 minutes. Teams see the alert where they already work, not in an alerting tool that no one looks at.

---

*If you want a detailed guide on deploying this stack on Kubernetes with Helm, it's in the Observability course available on the site.*

opensearch-33-nouveautes-operateur.titleEn: OpenSearch 3.3: what it changes for a platform operator
opensearch-33-nouveautes-operateur.excerptEn: I have been operating OpenSearch in production for 3 years, first on the Airbus ELK platform, now on a PaaS platform. Here's what 3.3 actually changes for someone who manages clusters on a daily basis.
opensearch-33-nouveautes-operateur.contentEn:
When OpenSearch releases a minor, I read the release notes like I read a post-mortem: looking for what will affect me in production. 3.3 is released in early 2025 with several announcements. Here is my filter operator.

## The real change: Unified Discover (preview)

The new Discover interface brings together logs, metrics and traces in a single view. It seems cosmetic, but it changes the workflow in incident.

**Before (OpenSearch 2.x):** During a P1 incident, I was juggling between three different tabs Discover for logs, Metrics Analytics for timeseries, and Trace Analytics for distributed tracing. Sticking a mental timeline between the three is useless cognitive work under stress.

**After:** a single view, immediate visual correlation. If a latency spike appears on the metrics at 2:03 p.m., I can directly see the corresponding logs and traces without changing tabs.

The feature is in **preview** in 3.3, stable expected in 3.4. I activated it on our staging environment:

```yaml
# opensearch_dashboards.yml
newUX.enabled: true
discover.newUX: true
```

My verdict after 2 weeks: the interface is faster than the old Discover on 50GB+ indexes, probably thanks to optimizations on the query side. Some display bugs on nested fields, but nothing blocking.

## Multiple data sources finally usable

The _Multiple Data Sources_ feature has existed since 2.x, but it was fragile. 3.3 really stabilizes it.

In our architecture, we have three OpenSearch clusters:
- `prod-eu-west` production logs and metrics
- `staging-cluster` testing environment
- `archive-cluster` archived logs > 90 days

Previously, comparing an error in production with its context in staging required two separate Dashboards, two tabs, two connections. Now:

```json
// opensearch_dashboards.yml (data sources)
{
  "dataSources": [
    {
      "id": "prod",
      "title": "Production EU",
      "endpoint": "https://opensearch-prod.internal:9200",
      "auth": { "type": "username_password" }
    },
    {
      "id": "staging",
      "title": "Staging",
      "endpoint": "https://opensearch-staging.internal:9200"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Operational use case:** when a dev tells me "it works in staging but not in production", I create a comparative dashboard with the two sources side by side. It takes 3 minutes instead of 20.

**Current limitation:** alerts cannot yet aggregate across multiple sources. If you have a rule "alert if error 500 > X on all clusters", you must always create an alert per cluster. It’s on the roadmap.

## Apache Calcite as PPL engine impact on existing queries

PPL (Piped Processing Language) is OpenSearch's pipe-style query language. 3.3 migrates the engine to Apache Calcite.

```ppl
# Exemple PPL   unchanged syntax, faster execution
source=logs
| where level = "ERROR"
| stats count() by service
| sort -count()
| head 10
```

The syntax does not change, but performance on complex aggregations improves significantly. Our analytics queries that used to take 8-12 seconds are dropping to 3-5 seconds on our production indexes.

**Point of attention:** some non-standard PPL functions may behave differently with Calcite. Run your favorite query suite on staging before migrating. We had a case of `strftime()` returning a slightly different date format.

## Agentic AI not for tomorrow in production, but to be monitored

OpenSearch 3.3 exposes _agentic search_ and _agentic memory_ APIs to plug LLMs into your data.

```python
# Exemple : question en langage naturel sur vos logs
client.search(
    index="logs-prod",
    body={
        "query": {
            "neural": {
                "content": {
                    "query_text": "quelles erreurs sont apparues après le déploiement de 14h ?",
                    "model_id": "amazon.titan-embed-text-v1"
                }
            }
        }
    }
)
```

Honestly, I don't yet see how to integrate this into a mature operational on-call workflow. LLMs are mind-blowing, and in P1 incident you want facts, not probabilistic suggestions. But for non-critical analytics (understanding a performance bug after the fact, summarizing a week of logs), it has potential.

I am monitoring adoption over the next 6 months before testing in real conditions.

## What really interests me for 3.4

- **Discover in GA** (not just preview)
- **Multi-source alerts** (critical lack for multi-cluster architectures)
- **Snapshot Management** improved the current is functional but verbose to configure

OpenSearch continues to catch up with Elasticsearch in terms of features. On the workloads I operate (logs, metrics, traces), 3.3 is a solid update. Migration recommended upon validation in staging.

---

*I operate OpenSearch via Kubernetes on a PaaS platform in production. If you have any questions about K8s deployment or multi-cluster architecture, comments are open.*

postmortem-base-de-donnees.titleEn: Post-mortem: 4 hours of unavailability due to a missing index
postmortem-base-de-donnees.excerptEn: How a seemingly innocuous database migration caused 4 hours of service degradation, and what we changed to make sure it never happens again.
postmortem-base-de-donnees.contentEn:
**Severity**: P1  
**Duration**: 4h12 (14:33 → 18:45 UTC)  
**Impacted services**: main API, customer portal  
**Users affected**: ~12,000

---

## Summary

A migration adding a new `tenant_id` column to a 45M row table generated a 7 second table lock, causing a cascade of timeouts and saturating the connection pool. Recovery took 4 hours due to a missing index on the new column, not detected before going live.

## Root cause

### What happened

The `20250302_add_tenant_id.sql` migration:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tenant_id UUID;
UPDATE orders SET tenant_id = '...'; -- default value pour 45M lignes
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN tenant_id SET NOT NULL;
```

In PostgreSQL < 14, `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` with `DEFAULT` locks the table while writing the value to all rows. Here: 7 seconds of exclusive lock on 45M lines.

### Why the index was missing

The application code systematically filters by `tenant_id`. Without index, each query does a sequential scan on 45M lines. With 200 req/s, the connection pool (20 connections max) found itself saturated in a few seconds.

```sql
-- La requête la plus fréquente, sans index :
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

-- Résultat : Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..890234.56 rows=12 width=384)
--            Actual time: 4231.456..4245.123 ms
```

### Why did it go to production

1. The staging environment only had 50k lines and the query took 12ms.
2. The migration review did not have a formal checklist.
3. No post-migration load testing.

---

## What we changed

### Short term

- Added missing index (done during the incident)
- Monitoring of `pg_stat_user_tables.seq_scan` to detect sequential scans

### Medium term

**1. Mandatory migration review checklist**

```markdown
## Checklist avant toute migration
- [ ] Volume de données en prod estimé
- [ ] Lock duration estimée et acceptable ?
- [ ] Indexes nécessaires créés AVANT la migration ?
- [ ] Plan de rollback testé
- [ ] Communication aux équipes dépendantes
```

**2. Safe migration template for large tables**

```sql
-- Pattern safe : backfill en batches
DO $$
DECLARE
  batch_size INT := 10000;
  offset_val INT := 0;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    UPDATE orders
    SET tenant_id = '...'
    WHERE id IN (
      SELECT id FROM orders
      WHERE tenant_id IS NULL
      LIMIT batch_size
    );
    EXIT WHEN NOT FOUND;
    PERFORM pg_sleep(0.1);
  END LOOP;
END $$;

-- Index CONCURRENTLY = pas de verrou de lecture
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_id ON orders(tenant_id);

-- Contrainte NOT NULL en dernier
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN tenant_id SET NOT NULL;
```

**3. Staging with real-size data**

We anonymize and load a production dump (10% by default, 100% for critical migrations).

## What we will never do again

> "The fact that it works in staging doesn't mean anything if staging doesn't have the same order of magnitude of data as prod."
